# Rawley Z. Heimer: research papers with abstracts and summaries
Updated November 2026. Source: https://rawleyheimer.com/research.html

## Dynamic Inconsistency in Risky Choice: Evidence from the Lab and Field

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer, Zwetelina Iliewa, Alex Imas, and Martin Weber
Status: American Economic Review 115 (1): 330–363 (2025)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/dynamic-inconsistency-risky-choice.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20210307
Topics: Retail investing and brokerage, Behavioral finance and beliefs

In brief: People’s plans for taking risk differ systematically from what they actually do once outcomes arrive. Using brokerage account data and a series of experiments, the paper shows that people typically plan to keep taking risk after gains and to stop after losses, but in practice they do the reverse: they cash out gains early and keep chasing losses. When offered a way to commit to their original plan, more people are willing to take the risk in the first place. The findings help reconcile why studies of one-shot gambles and studies of ongoing, repeated risk-taking often reach different conclusions about people’s appetite for risk.

Abstract: We document a robust dynamic inconsistency in risky choice. Using a unique brokerage dataset and a series of experiments, we compare people’s initial risk-taking plans to their subsequent decisions. Across settings, people accept risk as part of a “loss-exit” strategy — planning to continue taking risk after gains and stopping after losses. Actual behavior deviates from initial strategies by cutting gains early and chasing losses. More people accept risk when offered a commitment to their initial strategy. Our results help reconcile seemingly contradictory findings on risk-taking in static versus dynamic contexts. We explore implications for theory and welfare.

- Question: Do people follow through on their plans for taking risk once gains or losses arrive?
- Setting: Retail brokerage accounts and a series of experiments
- Data: A unique brokerage dataset and experimental choices
- Method: Comparison of people’s initial risk-taking plans with their later decisions, including when a commitment to the plan is offered
- Planned strategy: Keep taking risk after gains, stop after losses
- Actual behavior: Cash out gains early and chase losses
- Offering commitment to the plan: More people accept the risk

Keywords: dynamic inconsistency, risk-taking, loss chasing, realization of gains, commitment devices, prospect theory, brokerage data, lab experiments

BibTeX key: heimer2025dynamic

## Shale Shocked: Cash Windfalls and Household Debt Repayment

Authors: J. Anthony Cookson, Erik P. Gilje, and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Journal of Financial Economics 146 (3): 905–931 (2022)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/shale-shocked-cash-windfalls-household-debt.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2022.09.008
Topics: Consumer credit and debt, Saving, retirement, and inheritance

In brief: When households receive a sudden cash windfall, many use it to pay down debt rather than borrow more. Matching individual credit bureau records to royalty payments from shale oil and gas drilling (fracking), the paper finds that windfall recipients cut their debt-to-income ratio by 2.4 percentage points relative to similar people who received nothing, and the effect is three times larger for subprime borrowers than for prime borrowers. Repayment tracks when the cash actually arrives, not when people learn that future payments are coming. That pattern is hard to square with purely forward-looking models of borrowing, which predict that debt should rise after good news about future income.

Abstract: Using individual credit bureau data matched with cash windfalls from fracking, we estimate that windfall recipients reduce debt-to-income by 2.4 percentage points relative to no-windfall controls. Debt repayment effects are 3 times stronger for subprime individuals than for prime individuals. Based on the timing of upfront versus continuing cash payments, debt repayment coincides with the timing of payments but not with news about future payments. These findings present a challenge for purely forward-looking models of debt. Indeed, when we incorporate a windfall shock into a forward-looking model, the model predicts an increase in debt that runs counter to our evidence of debt repayment.

- Question: Do households use cash windfalls to borrow more or to pay down debt?
- Setting: Royalty payments from shale oil and gas drilling (fracking)
- Data: Individual credit bureau records matched to windfall payments
- Method: Recipients compared with similar no-windfall controls; timing of upfront versus continuing payments
- Debt-to-income of windfall recipients: −2.4 pp
- Repayment effect, subprime relative to prime: 3 times larger
- Repayment timed to: Cash receipt, not news

Keywords: cash windfalls, household debt, debt repayment, fracking, shale royalties, credit bureau data, subprime borrowers, permanent income hypothesis

BibTeX key: heimer2022shale

## Biased by Choice: How Financial Constraints Can Reduce Financial Mistakes

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer and Alex Imas
Status: Review of Financial Studies 35 (4): 1643–1681 (2022)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/biased-by-choice-financial-constraints.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhab073
Topics: Retail investing and brokerage, Behavioral finance and beliefs, Consumer protection and financial regulation

In brief: Limits on borrowing can make investors better off by curbing their behavioral biases. Studying a regulation that restricted how much leverage retail traders could use, the paper finds that constrained traders had better market timing and a weaker disposition effect — the tendency to sell winners too soon and hold on to losers. The mechanism is opportunity cost: when borrowing is limited, keeping a losing position open ties up capital that could fund new trades, so putting off a loss becomes more expensive. Two separate experiments reproduce the result, suggesting that well-designed constraints can work as a form of choice architecture.

Abstract: We show that constraints can improve financial decision-making by disciplining behavioral biases. In financial markets, restrictions on leverage limit traders’ ability to borrow to open new positions. We demonstrate that regulation that restricts the provision of leverage to retail traders improves trading performance. By increasing the opportunity cost of postponing the realization of losses, leverage constraints improve traders’ market timing and reduce their disposition effect. We replicate these findings in two distinct experimental settings, further isolating the mechanism and demonstrating generality of the results. The interaction between constraints and behavioral biases has implications for policy and choice architecture.

- Question: Can limits on borrowing reduce investors’ behavioral biases?
- Setting: A regulation restricting the leverage available to retail traders
- Data: Retail trading records and two experimental settings
- Method: Trading before and after the leverage restriction; replication in two experiments
- Trading performance: Improves under leverage constraints
- Market timing: Improves
- Disposition effect: Declines
- Mechanism: Constraints raise the opportunity cost of postponing realized losses

Keywords: leverage constraints, disposition effect, behavioral biases, retail traders, financial regulation, choice architecture, experiments

BibTeX key: heimer2022biased

## Personal Wealth, Self-Employment, and Business Ownership

Authors: Aymeric Bellon, J. Anthony Cookson, Erik P. Gilje, and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Review of Financial Studies 34 (8): 3935–3975 (2021)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/personal-wealth-self-employment-business-ownership.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhab044
Topics: Saving, retirement, and inheritance

In brief: Does having more money make people more likely to start a business? Using mineral payments from Texas shale drilling to individuals across the United States, the paper finds that large cash windfalls raise business formation by 0.8 to 2.1 percentage points but do not make people more likely to become self-employed. Windfalls do let people who are already self-employed stay self-employed longer, while having no effect on how long business owners keep their businesses. Liquidity constraints therefore matter differently depending on what motivates the would-be entrepreneur, which helps reconcile conflicting results in earlier research.

Abstract: We study the effect of personal wealth on entrepreneurial decisions using data on mineral payments from Texas shale drilling to individuals throughout the United States. Large cash windfalls increase business formation by 0.8 to 2.1 percentage points, but do not affect transitions to self-employment. By contrast, cash windfalls significantly extend self-employment spells, but do not affect the duration of business ownership. Our findings help reconcile contrasting findings in prior work: liquidity constraints have different effects on entrepreneurial activity that may depend on the entrepreneur’s motivations.

- Question: Does personal wealth lead people to start businesses or become self-employed?
- Setting: Mineral payments from Texas shale drilling to individuals across the United States
- Method: Large cash windfalls as variation in personal wealth
- Business formation: +0.8 to 2.1 pp
- Transitions to self-employment: No effect
- Length of self-employment spells: Longer
- Duration of business ownership: No effect

Keywords: entrepreneurship, liquidity constraints, business formation, self-employment, cash windfalls, shale royalties, personal wealth

BibTeX key: heimer2021personal

## Politicizing Consumer Credit

Authors: Pat Akey, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Stefan Lewellen
Status: Journal of Financial Economics 139 (2): 627–655 (2021)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/politicizing-consumer-credit.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2020.07.017
Topics: Consumer protection and financial regulation, Consumer credit and debt, Mortgage lending and housing

In brief: Political power can weaken the enforcement of fair-lending rules, and lenders respond. When a state’s senator becomes chair of a Senate committee, credit access to minority neighborhoods in that state falls by 7.5%. The declines are larger in neighborhoods eligible under the Community Reinvestment Act and when the senator’s committee oversees fair-lending enforcement, and they are driven by banks headquartered in the senator’s home state. Expected regulatory relief, not only formal changes to the rules, shapes who gets credit.

Abstract: Powerful politicians can interfere with the enforcement of regulations. As such, expected political interference can affect constituents’ behavior. Using rotations of Senate committee chairs to identify variation in political power and expected regulatory relief, we study powerful politicians’ effect on consumer lending to communities protected by fair-lending regulations. We find a 7.5% reduction in credit access to minority neighborhoods in states with new committee chairs. Larger reductions occur in Community Reinvestment Act-eligible neighborhoods and when Senators serve on committees that oversee the enforcement of fair-lending laws. Banks headquartered in powerful Senators’ states are responsible for the reduction in credit access.

- Question: Does expected political interference with regulation change who gets credit?
- Setting: Rotations of U.S. Senate committee chairs
- Data: Lending to communities protected by fair-lending regulations
- Method: New committee chairs as variation in political power and expected regulatory relief
- Credit access in minority neighborhoods: −7.5% in states with new committee chairs
- Larger declines: Community Reinvestment Act-eligible neighborhoods; senators on committees overseeing fair-lending enforcement
- Source of the decline: Banks headquartered in the senator’s state

Keywords: fair lending, Community Reinvestment Act, political economy, Senate committee chairs, regulatory enforcement, minority neighborhoods, credit access, mortgage lending

BibTeX key: heimer2021politicizing

## YOLO: Mortality Beliefs and Household Finance Puzzles

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer, Kristian Ove R. Myrseth, and Raphael S. Schoenle
Status: Journal of Finance 74 (6): 2957–2996 (2019)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/yolo-mortality-beliefs-household-finance.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12828
Topics: Saving, retirement, and inheritance, Behavioral finance and beliefs

In brief: People’s beliefs about how long they will live are systematically off, and this helps explain why the young save too little and retirees spend down their savings too slowly. New survey evidence shows that young people underestimate their chances of survival while older people overestimate theirs. Feeding these beliefs into a standard life-cycle model, the young under-save by 26% and retirees draw down assets 27% more slowly than they would using actuarial survival odds, and the model’s fit to real consumption data improves by 88%. The distortions are linked to overweighting the likelihood of rare events.

Abstract: We study the effect of subjective mortality beliefs on life-cycle behavior. With new survey evidence, we document that survival is underestimated by the young and overestimated by the old. We calibrate a canonical life-cycle model to elicited beliefs. Relative to calibrations using actuarial probabilities, the young under-save by 26%, and retirees draw down their assets 27% slower, while the model’s fit to consumption data improves by 88%. Cross-sectional regressions support the model’s predictions: distorted mortality beliefs correlate with savings behavior while controlling for risk preferences, cognitive, and socioeconomic factors. Overweighting the likelihood of rare events contributes to mortality belief distortions.

- Question: How do people’s beliefs about their own survival affect saving and spending over the life cycle?
- Data: New survey evidence on subjective survival beliefs
- Method: A canonical life-cycle model calibrated to elicited beliefs versus actuarial probabilities; cross-sectional regressions
- Saving by the young: 26% lower
- Asset drawdown by retirees: 27% slower
- Model fit to consumption data: 88% better

Keywords: subjective mortality beliefs, life expectancy, life-cycle model, retirement saving, undersaving, asset decumulation, probability weighting, survey evidence

BibTeX key: heimer2019yolo

## Should Retail Investors’ Leverage Be Limited?

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer and Alp Simsek
Status: Journal of Financial Economics 132 (3): 1–21 (2019)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/should-retail-investors-leverage-be-limited.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2018.10.017
Topics: Retail investing and brokerage, Consumer protection and financial regulation

In brief: Capping how much leverage retail traders can use made them better off without harming market liquidity. The paper studies 2010 U.S. rules that limited leverage in the retail foreign exchange (forex) market. The cap cut trading volume by 23%, reduced high-leverage traders’ losses by 40%, and shrank brokerages’ operating capital by 25%, yet brokerages did not raise the bid-ask spreads they charged. The authors conclude that the policy improved (belief-neutral) social welfare without reducing market liquidity.

Abstract: Does the provision of leverage to retail traders improve market quality or facilitate socially inefficient speculation that enriches financial intermediaries? We evaluate the effects of 2010 regulations that cap leverage in the U.S. retail foreign exchange market. Using three unique data sets and a difference-in-differences approach, we document that the leverage constraint reduces trading volume by 23%, alleviates high-leverage traders’ losses by 40%, and reduces brokerages’ operating capital by 25%. Yet, the policy does not affect the relative bid-ask prices charged by the brokerages. These results suggest the policy improves belief-neutral social welfare without reducing market liquidity.

- Question: Does giving retail traders access to leverage improve market quality, or does it mainly fund speculation that enriches intermediaries?
- Setting: 2010 U.S. regulations capping leverage in the retail foreign exchange market
- Data: Three unique data sets
- Method: Difference-in-differences
- Trading volume: −23%
- Losses of high-leverage traders: −40%
- Brokerages’ operating capital: −25%
- Relative bid-ask prices charged by brokerages: No effect

Keywords: leverage limits, retail forex trading, Dodd-Frank, speculation, financial regulation, market liquidity, brokerages, difference-in-differences

BibTeX key: heimer2019leverage

## Growing Up Without Finance

Authors: James R. Brown, J. Anthony Cookson, and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Journal of Financial Economics 134 (3): 591–616 (2019)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/growing-up-without-finance.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.05.006
Topics: Consumer credit and debt, Legal institutions and financial development

In brief: Growing up near banks and other financial institutions has lasting benefits for people’s financial lives. Congressional legislation created unintended differences in financial development across Native American reservations, which the paper uses to isolate the effect of local financial markets. People from financially underdeveloped reservations enter credit markets later and, as adults, have credit scores about 10 points lower and 4 percentage points more delinquent accounts; these effects fade only slowly even after they move to more developed areas. Early exposure to local banking appears to work by building financial literacy and trust in financial institutions.

Abstract: Early-life exposure to local financial institutions increases household financial inclusion and leads to long-term improvements in consumer credit outcomes. We identify the effect of local financial markets using Congressional legislation that led to unintended differences in financial market development across Native American reservations. Individuals from financially underdeveloped reservations enter consumer credit markets later, and upon reaching adulthood, have 10 point lower credit scores and 4 percentage point more delinquent accounts. These effects are long-lived and depreciate slowly after individuals move to more developed areas. Formative exposures to local banking improve consumer credit behavior by increasing financial literacy and financial trust.

- Question: Does early-life exposure to local financial institutions shape consumer credit outcomes in adulthood?
- Setting: Congressional legislation that created unintended differences in financial development across Native American reservations
- Data: Individual-level consumer credit records
- Method: People from financially underdeveloped versus more developed reservations, including after they move
- Credit scores as adults: About 10 points lower
- Delinquent accounts: 4 pp more
- Entry into credit markets: Later
- Persistence after moving away: Fades slowly

Keywords: financial inclusion, financial development, credit scores, financial literacy, trust in banks, Native American reservations, early-life exposure, consumer credit

BibTeX key: heimer2019growing

## Law and Finance Matter: Lessons from Externally Imposed Courts

Authors: James R. Brown, J. Anthony Cookson, and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Review of Financial Studies 30 (3): 1019–1051 (2017)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/law-and-finance-matter-externally-imposed-courts.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhw030
Topics: Legal institutions and financial development

In brief: Predictable contract enforcement leads to stronger credit markets and higher incomes. When Congress assigned state courts, rather than tribal courts, to adjudicate contracts on some Native American reservations, it created lasting differences in how predictably contracts were enforced. Reservations under state courts have stronger small-business and household credit markets. The part of credit market development driven by this legal difference is associated with significantly higher per capita income, especially in sectors that depend more on outside financing.

Abstract: This paper provides novel evidence on the real and financial market effects of legal institutions. Our analysis exploits persistent and externally imposed differences in court enforcement that arose when the U.S. Congress assigned state courts to adjudicate contracts on a subset of Native American reservations. Using area-specific data on small business and household credit, reservations assigned to state courts, which enforce contracts more predictably than tribal courts, have stronger credit markets. Moreover, the law-driven component of credit market development is associated with significantly higher per capita income, with stronger effects in sectors that depend more on external financing.

- Question: Does predictable contract enforcement strengthen credit markets and raise incomes?
- Setting: Congress’s assignment of state rather than tribal courts to adjudicate contracts on a subset of Native American reservations
- Data: Area-specific data on small business and household credit
- Method: Reservations assigned to state courts compared with those that kept tribal courts
- Credit markets under state courts: Stronger
- Per capita income: Significantly higher where law-driven credit development is greater
- Where effects are largest: Sectors that depend more on external financing

Keywords: law and finance, contract enforcement, legal institutions, credit markets, economic growth, tribal courts, state courts, Native American reservations

BibTeX key: heimer2017law

## Peer Pressure: Social Interaction and the Disposition Effect

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Review of Financial Studies 29 (11): 3177–3209 (2016)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/peer-pressure-social-interaction-disposition-effect.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhw063
Topics: Retail investing and brokerage, Behavioral finance and beliefs

In brief: Social interaction makes investors more prone to the disposition effect — selling winning positions too soon and holding on to losers. Using an investment-focused social network linked to individual trading records, and exploiting the staggered timing with which brokerages partnered with the platform, the paper finds that gaining access to the network nearly doubles a trader’s disposition effect. Traders who are connected in the network develop similar levels of the bias, a pattern that also shows up in standard data from a large discount brokerage.

Abstract: Social interaction contributes to some traders’ disposition effect. New data from an investment-specific social network linked to individual-level trading records builds evidence of this connection. To credibly estimate causal peer effects, I exploit the staggered entry of retail brokerages into partnerships with the social trading web platform and compare trader activity before and after exposure to these new social conditions. Access to the social network nearly doubles the magnitude of a trader’s disposition effect. Traders connected in the network develop correlated levels of the disposition effect, a finding that can be replicated using workhorse data from a large discount brokerage.

- Question: Does social interaction make investors more prone to the disposition effect?
- Setting: An investment-specific social network linked to individual trading records
- Data: Social network activity and trading records; data from a large discount brokerage
- Method: Staggered entry of retail brokerages into partnerships with the social trading platform
- Disposition effect after network access: Nearly doubles
- Traders connected in the network: Develop correlated levels of the bias

Keywords: disposition effect, peer effects, social interaction, social trading networks, retail traders, behavioral finance

BibTeX key: heimer2016peer

## Financial Decision Making, at the Dawn of AI

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Economics and Finance, forthcoming (2026)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/financial-decision-making-dawn-of-ai.html
Topics: Behavioral finance and beliefs

In brief: A review of research on how people make personal financial decisions, and of how generative AI might change them. A review of research on how people make personal financial decisions — saving versus spending, investing, and borrowing — and why their choices often depart from what financial economics prescribes. The article surveys the main drivers of those departures in each domain. It closes with a forward-looking discussion of how generative AI might reshape the way individuals make financial decisions.

Abstract: This article gives perspective on the academic literature on personal financial decision making. I explore three main domains of financial choices: savings versus consumption, investment decision making, and choices around debt. In each domain, people behave in ways that deviate from normative prescriptions of financial economics. I explore the main drivers of financial decisions that result in these deviations. The article concludes with a forward-looking perspective of how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) might reshape the landscape of individual’s financial decisions.

Keywords: household finance, personal financial decision making, generative AI, saving and consumption, investment mistakes, debt choices, behavioral finance survey

BibTeX key: heimer2026ai

## Subjective Beliefs, Saving, and Spending for Retirement

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Chapter in Retirement Saving, Investment, and Spending: New Lessons from Behavioral Research, edited by Olivia S. Mitchell and Nikolai Roussanov, Oxford University Press (2026)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/subjective-beliefs-saving-spending-retirement.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780197845752.003.0003
Topics: Saving, retirement, and inheritance, Behavioral finance and beliefs

In brief: People plan for retirement using their own beliefs about the future, and those beliefs often differ from the objective probabilities that economists and financial planners build into their models. This chapter reviews research on how people form such beliefs and how using them changes the conclusions of a standard life-cycle model of saving and spending. It focuses on one especially consequential gap: what people believe about their own chances of survival.

Abstract: Beliefs about future events are crucial to the decisions that people make when developing financial plans over the life cycle. Yet peoples’ subjective beliefs can often differ from the objective probabilities that economists and financial planners use in their models. This chapter discusses findings on subjective beliefs, how people might form their beliefs, and how these beliefs affect conclusions drawn from a classical economic life-cycle model. The author highlights a specific divergence between subjective beliefs and objective probabilities: subjective beliefs about peoples’ mortality. Incorporating these subjective mortality beliefs into standard models helps explain observed financial behaviors, including under-saving for retirement and increased risk taking, that are difficult to reconcile using actuarial probabilities alone.

Keywords: subjective beliefs, retirement saving, retirement spending, mortality beliefs, life-cycle model, financial planning

BibTeX key: heimer2026subjective

## Courting Economic Development

Authors: James R. Brown, J. Anthony Cookson, and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: World Bank Economic Review 30 (Supplement 1): S176–S187 (2017)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/courting-economic-development.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/wber/lhw027
Topics: Legal institutions and financial development

In brief: Uncertainty about how courts will enforce contracts holds back economic development. A 1953 federal law gave state courts authority over civil disputes on some Native American reservations, while tribal courts kept that authority on others. Although the two groups of reservations were economically similar when the law passed, those under state courts grew significantly faster over the long run. The gap is driven by the poorest reservations with tribal courts, and specifically by those where court enforcement was most uncertain.

Abstract: We show that court enforcement uncertainty hinders economic development using sharp variation in judiciaries across Native American reservations in the United States. Congressional legislation passed in 1953 assigned state courts the authority to resolve civil disputes on a subset of reservations, while tribal courts retained authority on unaffected reservations. Although affected and unaffected reservations had similar economic conditions when the law passed, reservations under state courts experienced significantly greater long-run growth. When we examine the distribution of incomes across reservations, the average difference in development is due to the lower incomes of the most impoverished reservations with tribal courts. We show that the relative under-development of reservations with tribal courts is driven by reservations with the most uncertainty in court enforcement.

- Question: Does uncertainty in court enforcement hold back economic development?
- Setting: A 1953 federal law giving state courts civil jurisdiction on some Native American reservations
- Data: Long-run income across reservations
- Method: Reservations under state courts compared with economically similar reservations that kept tribal courts
- Long-run growth under state courts: Significantly greater
- Source of the gap: Lower incomes on the poorest reservations with tribal courts
- Where the gap is largest: Reservations with the most uncertain court enforcement

Keywords: economic development, court enforcement, legal uncertainty, tribal courts, Public Law 280, Native American reservations, income growth

BibTeX key: heimer2015courting

## Friends Do Let Friends Buy Stocks Actively

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 107 (Part B): 527–540 (2014)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/friends-do-let-friends-buy-stocks-actively.html
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.04.019
Topics: Retail investing and brokerage, Behavioral finance and beliefs

In brief: Sociable people are more likely to be active traders than passive investors. Earlier work linked sociability to stock market participation but could not tell which kinds of investors were more social. Using Consumer Expenditure Survey data on individuals’ asset holdings, trading, and spending patterns that indicate social activity, the paper finds that social interaction is more common among active investors than passive ones. This supports an explanation for the active investing puzzle in which word-of-mouth communication tends to spread active rather than passive strategies.

Abstract: This research is the first to provide empirical evidence that social interaction is more prevalent amongst active rather than passive investors. While previous empirical work, spearheaded by Hong, Kubik, and Stein (2004), shows that proxies for sociability are related to participation in asset markets, the literature is unable to distinguish between the types of participants because of data limitations. I address this shortcoming by using data from the Consumer Expenditure Quarterly Interview Survey on individual holdings, and buying and selling of financial assets as well as expenditure variables which imply variation in the level of social activity. My findings support a new explanation for the active investing puzzle in which informal communication tends to promote active rather than passive strategies (Han and Hirshleifer 2012).

- Question: Are sociable people more likely to be active or passive investors?
- Data: Consumer Expenditure Quarterly Interview Survey: asset holdings, trading, and spending that indicates social activity
- Method: Proxies for social activity related to active versus passive investing
- Social interaction: More prevalent among active than passive investors
- Implication: Word of mouth tends to spread active rather than passive strategies

Keywords: active investing puzzle, social interaction, stock market participation, word of mouth, passive investing, Consumer Expenditure Survey

BibTeX key: heimer2014friends

## Facebook Finance: How Social Interaction Propagates Active Investing

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer and David Simon
Status: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Working Paper 15-22 (2015)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/facebook-finance-social-interaction-active-investing.html
Topics: Retail investing and brokerage, Behavioral finance and beliefs

In brief: Active trading strategies spread through social networks of retail investors. Using a social network for traders linked to individual trading records, the paper finds that traders who do well in the short run reach out to others, and that traders trade more when their peers perform well and communicate more. The staggered entry of brokerages into partnerships with the network supports a causal interpretation. This communication pattern promotes active trading even though the network itself reveals how rarely retail traders succeed.

Abstract: This paper shows how active investing strategies propagate through social connections in a network of retail traders, using a new database of social activity linked to individual-level trading records. A trader’s good short-term performance causes them to contact others. A trader’s activity increases when peers perform well and increase communication. We use the staggered entry of brokerages into partnerships with the social networking platform, which is a necessary precursor for traders to access the network, to argue these effects are causal. This pattern of communication supports active trading, even though the network reveals the low success rate of retail traders.

- Question: How do active investing strategies spread through social networks?
- Data: A new database of social activity linked to individual-level trading records
- Method: Staggered entry of brokerages into partnerships with the social networking platform
- Traders with good short-term performance: Contact others
- When peers perform well and communicate more: A trader’s activity increases
- Net effect: Communication supports active trading despite low success rates

Keywords: social networks, active trading, retail traders, peer effects, social transmission, investor communication

BibTeX key: heimer2015facebook

## Temporal Focal Points and Economic Outcomes: Evidence from U.S. Mortgage Lending

Authors: Marco Giacoletti, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Edison Yu
Status: Working paper (2021)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/temporal-focal-points-mortgage-lending.html
Topics: Mortgage lending and housing, Consumer protection and financial regulation

In brief: Monthly volume quotas for loan officers reveal how much of the racial gap in mortgage approvals stems from lender behavior. Studying 25 years of mortgage lending, the authors develop a new test for disparate treatment: approval rates rise at the end of each month as loan officers try to hit their quotas, and they estimate these quotas at least halve the unexplained 7-percentage-point gap in approval rates for Black applicants. Loan officers more likely to miss their quotas show larger increases in Black approvals. Because applications arrive at a steady rate through the month and neither credit risk nor applicant preferences explain the pattern, the evidence points to supply-side (lender) mechanisms.

Abstract: We develop modified benchmarking tests for disparate treatment that we apply to 25 years of mortgage lending. Our tests limit the scope for omitted variables by linking high-frequency mortgage decisions to an economic mechanism — loan officers have volume quotas that cause increased approval rates at month-end. We estimate that these quotas at least halve the unexplained 7 ppt Black approval gap. Loan officers more likely to miss their quotas have larger increases in Black approvals. Suggesting supply-side mechanisms, applications arrive at a constant rate within-month, and neither differences in credit risk nor applicant preferences explain the month-end decline in racial differences.

- Question: How much of the racial gap in mortgage approvals reflects lender behavior?
- Setting: Loan officers’ monthly volume quotas, which raise approval rates at the end of each month
- Data: 25 years of U.S. mortgage lending
- Method: Modified benchmarking tests for disparate treatment that link high-frequency lending decisions to month-end quotas
- Unexplained gap in Black approval rates: 7 pp
- Share of the gap the quota effect closes: At least half
- Loan officers more likely to miss quotas: Larger increases in Black approvals
- Alternative explanations: Applications arrive steadily within the month; credit risk and applicant preferences do not explain the pattern

Keywords: mortgage lending, racial disparities, disparate treatment, discrimination testing, loan officer quotas, month-end effects, HMDA

BibTeX key: heimer2021temporal

## Fallible Firms: The Economics of Consumer Redress

Authors: Charlotte Haendler and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Working paper (2025)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/fallible-firms-consumer-redress.html
Topics: Consumer protection and financial regulation, Consumer credit and debt

In brief: Who gets money back after complaining about a financial company depends heavily on who is complaining. Using confidential Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) data on nearly two million complaints filed since 2014, the paper finds that successful complaints pay out $1,470 on average and that total restitution has grown substantially over time. Differences across firms explain little; instead, higher-income and more educated consumers are more likely to request refunds, allege fraud, and submit documentation, and firms respond to them more. CFPB monitoring raises restitution but disproportionately benefits these higher-socioeconomic-status consumers.

Abstract: Financial disputes are a widespread but understudied feature of consumer financial markets. Using confidential data from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), we analyze nearly two million consumer complaints filed since 2014, which have led to an average payout of $1,470 per successful complaint. The volume of complaints and total restitution have increased substantially over time, suggesting significant scope for additional compensation. When understanding who secures restitution — and why — we find little evidence that differences across firms systematically drive restitution outcomes. Instead, product complexity and consumer engagement play key roles: consumers with higher income and education (high-SES) are more likely to explicitly request refunds, claim fraud, and submit supporting documentation, making firms more responsive. Leveraging previously unexamined CFPB monitoring reviews, where the agency systematically screens company responses and issues confidential reports highlighting deficiencies, we show that regulatory scrutiny increases restitution but disproportionately benefits high-SES consumers, reinforcing individual-specific mechanisms. Our results highlight the complementary nature of regulatory interventions and suggest that financial sophistication and self-advocacy are critical determinants of consumer redress.

- Question: Who secures restitution after a complaint about a financial company, and why?
- Setting: Consumer complaints filed with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau since 2014
- Data: Confidential CFPB data on nearly two million complaints, including CFPB monitoring reviews of company responses
- Method: Restitution outcomes across firms, products, and consumer characteristics; effects of CFPB monitoring reviews
- Average payout per successful complaint: $1,470
- Differences across firms: Explain little of who gets restitution
- Higher-income, more educated consumers: More likely to request refunds, claim fraud, and document complaints
- CFPB monitoring reviews: Raise restitution, disproportionately for higher-income, more educated consumers

Keywords: consumer complaints, CFPB, financial restitution, consumer redress, financial sophistication, regulatory supervision, consumer protection

BibTeX key: heimer2025fallible

## Pushing Boundaries: Political Redistricting and Consumer Credit

Authors: Pat Akey, Christine Dobridge, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Stefan Lewellen
Status: Working paper (2017)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/pushing-boundaries-redistricting-consumer-credit.html
Topics: Consumer credit and debt, Consumer protection and financial regulation

In brief: Gerrymandering reduces people’s access to credit. Matching a long-running panel of consumer credit data to changes in congressional district boundaries after each census, the paper finds that consumers lose access to credit when their districts are irregularly redrawn to favor a political party. The losses are concentrated in states where elected politicians draw the maps and in districts whose later elections are less competitive, and similar declines follow gerrymandered state senate maps and laws that make voting harder. The results fit theories in which less competitive races weaken politicians’ incentives to serve their constituents.

Abstract: Consumers lose access to credit when their congressional district boundaries are irregularly redrawn to benefit a political party (i.e., are gerrymandered). We identify this effect by matching a longitudinal panel of consumer credit data with changes in congressional district boundaries following decennial censuses. Reductions in credit access are concentrated in states that allow elected politicians to draw political boundaries and in districts where subsequent congressional elections are less competitive. We find similar reductions in credit access when state senate district boundaries are irregularly redrawn and when states make it more difficult for constituents to vote. Overall, our findings are consistent with theories suggesting that less-competitive political races reduce politicians’ incentives to cater to their constituents’ preferences.

- Question: Does gerrymandering reduce people’s access to credit?
- Setting: Changes in congressional district boundaries after each decennial census
- Data: A longitudinal panel of consumer credit data
- Method: Consumers whose districts are irregularly redrawn compared with others
- Credit access after gerrymandering: Falls
- Larger declines: States where elected politicians draw the maps; districts with less competitive elections
- Similar declines: Gerrymandered state senate maps; laws that make voting harder

Keywords: gerrymandering, redistricting, consumer credit, credit access, political competition, voting restrictions, political economy

BibTeX key: heimer2017pushing

## Five Facts about Bequest Motives

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer and Xiang Li
Status: Working paper (2025)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/five-facts-bequest-motives.html
Topics: Saving, retirement, and inheritance

In brief: Using three decades of survey data, the paper documents five facts about how people think about leaving an inheritance. People with heirs care more about bequests; the importance of bequests follows a U-shape over the life cycle; it rises sharply among the wealthiest fifth of households; stock owners, especially those who have enjoyed high market returns, care more about bequests; and people systematically overestimate how likely and how large their bequests will be. These facts give economic models new benchmarks and suggest that bequest motives change over time rather than staying fixed. The paper also works through what the facts imply for wealth accumulation and portfolio choice in a life-cycle model.

Abstract: Rising differences in generational wealth and the economic effects of inheritances make it increasingly important to understand individuals’ bequest motives. We document five novel empirical facts about individuals’ preferences and expectations toward bequests using survey data spanning three decades. (1) Households with heirs exhibit stronger bequest preferences. (2) Bequest motives follow a U-shaped pattern over the life cycle. (3) The perceived importance of bequests rises sharply among the top two deciles of the wealth distribution. (4) Stock owners, particularly those who experience high market returns, report stronger bequest preferences. (5) Individuals systematically overestimate their bequests’ likelihood and size. These stylized facts provide new benchmarks for evaluating economic models and suggest that alternatives to the static treatment of bequest motives may better reflect observed behavior. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for wealth accumulation and portfolio choice within a canonical life-cycle model with precautionary savings.

- Question: What do people’s preferences and expectations about leaving bequests look like?
- Data: Survey data spanning three decades
- Method: Stylized facts, with implications examined in a life-cycle model with precautionary saving
- Fact 1: Households with heirs have stronger bequest preferences
- Fact 2: Bequest motives follow a U-shape over the life cycle
- Fact 3: The importance of bequests rises sharply in the top two wealth deciles
- Fact 4: Stock owners, especially after high returns, have stronger bequest preferences
- Fact 5: People overestimate how likely and how large their bequests will be

Keywords: bequest motives, inheritances, intergenerational wealth, life-cycle model, wealth inequality, portfolio choice, subjective expectations

BibTeX key: heimer2025bequest

## The Wealth Draw-down of the Fabulously Rich: Insights from Private Family Foundations

Authors: Changhyun Ahn and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Working paper, draft available on request
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/wealth-drawdown-private-family-foundations.html
Topics: Saving, retirement, and inheritance

In brief: When the eldest member of a very wealthy family dies, the family’s private foundation roughly doubles in size within two years, the opposite of the gradual late-life drawdown that standard life-cycle models predict. Linking IRS filings for the universe of U.S. private foundations to genealogical records, the paper tracks 8,276 family foundations holding an average of $20.65 million in assets. Charitable giving lags far behind the post-death inflows, which come mostly from surviving family trustees and often as noncash assets, and foundations become more likely to fall below the five-percent payout requirement. After the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act doubled the estate and gift tax exemption, post-death inflows fell by 47.2%, suggesting many families use foundations to manage estate taxes.

Abstract: We connect genealogical records to the universe of 501(c)(3) private foundations to provide novel insights into the late-in-life assets holdings and charitable contributions of the wealthiest households in the U.S. This linkage allows us to track life-cycle financial assets and charitable disbursements for 8,276 families, each holding an average of $20.65 million in family foundation assets annually. In contrast to life-cycle models that predict a steady draw-down of assets late in life, we find that the death of the eldest family member leads to a 96.9% increase in foundation assets within two years. Yet few are prepared to distribute their wealth postmortem — charitable disbursements take years to match post-death inflows and funds are more likely to fall below the five-percent rule to qualify for non-profit status. We also find that the doubling of the lifetime estate and gift tax exemption in the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act caused a 47.2% reduction in postmortem inflows into family foundations, which suggests that many family foundations are used to reduce estate taxes. These findings contribute to our understanding of inter-generational wealth inequality.

- Question: How do the wealthiest families draw down assets late in life, and how much reaches charity?
- Setting: The universe of U.S. 501(c)(3) private foundations linked to genealogical records
- Data: IRS Form 990-PF filings and NCCS data, 2000–2023; 8,276 family foundations
- Method: Staggered difference-in-differences around deaths of the eldest family member, compared with asset-matched foundations
- Foundation assets within two years of a death: +96.9%
- Charitable outflows: Rise slowly
- Likelihood of meeting the 5% payout rule: Falls
- Post-death inflows after the 2017 tax law: −47.2%

Keywords: private family foundations, intergenerational wealth inequality, bequest motives, charitable giving, estate taxation, Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, donor-advised funds

BibTeX key: heimer2025foundations

## Single-Family REITs and Local Housing Markets

Authors: Marco Giacoletti, Rawley Z. Heimer, Wenli Li, and Edison Yu
Status: Working paper (2024)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/single-family-reits-local-housing-markets.html
Topics: Mortgage lending and housing

In brief: Large institutional landlords in single-family housing are often blamed for hurting households, but this paper finds little evidence that they cause harm. Building a new dataset of the homes owned by single-family REITs, the authors show these firms buy in neighborhoods ringing city centers, where housing supply is more elastic and residents face barriers to homeownership. REIT growth is associated with more housing supply, lower mortgage approval rates, and modest price increases, though these patterns likely reflect where REITs choose to buy rather than effects they cause. Returns on REIT housing portfolios mirror those of representative housing portfolios despite their concentrated holdings.

Abstract: Institutional investors in single-family housing markets are often represented as worsening household well-being. We document the growth of single-family REITs (SFRs) and their (non-)effects on housing markets by constructing a novel dataset of SFRs’ underlying properties. SFRs purchase properties in neighborhoods encircling city centers, where housing supply is more elastic, and with populations facing homeownership barriers. Using a spatial differences empirical strategy, SFR growth relates to increased housing supply, lower mortgage approval rates, and modest price increases. These findings likely capture SFRs’ selection of neighborhoods rather than causal effects. SFR asset returns mirror representative housing portfolios despite their concentrated holdings.

- Question: Do institutional landlords in single-family housing harm local housing markets?
- Data: A new dataset of the properties owned by single-family REITs
- Method: Spatial differences
- Where REITs buy: Neighborhoods encircling city centers, with elastic housing supply and barriers to homeownership
- Associated with REIT growth: More housing supply, lower mortgage approval rates, modest price increases
- Interpretation: Likely reflects where REITs choose to buy rather than causal effects
- REIT returns: Mirror representative housing portfolios

Keywords: single-family rental, institutional investors, REITs, housing supply, house prices, homeownership, mortgage approvals

BibTeX key: heimer2024reits

## Brokerage Commissions and Trading Volume: Lessons from the 20th Century

Authors: Valeria Fedyk and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Working paper, draft available on request
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/brokerage-commissions-trading-volume.html
Topics: Retail investing and brokerage

In brief: When the New York Stock Exchange set brokerage commissions, higher commissions led to more trading, not less. Before commissions were deregulated in 1975, NYSE minimum commissions were a fixed function of a stock’s price, with kinks in the schedule and periodic revisions. Exploiting both, the paper finds that a 1% increase in commissions raised trading volume by roughly 0.15% to 0.40%, with effects concentrated in more volatile stocks. The authors attribute this to brokers: fixed schedules limited price competition and gave brokers the incentive and room to steer naïve investors toward high-commission stocks.

Abstract: We ask how brokerage commissions affect trading activity. Estimating this causal effect is difficult because commissions are typically endogenous to the market. We turn to the pre-1976 era, when the New York Stock Exchange set and repeatedly revised minimum commission schedules, with commission rates a deterministic function of a stock’s price. This institutional feature delivers two complementary identification strategies. First, we exploit discontinuities in the price-based commission schedule in a regression kink design: higher commission rates raise trading volume, with a 1% increase in commissions increasing volume by approximately between 0.15% and 0.40%. Second, we exploit discrete changes in the schedule in a difference-in-differences design around rule revisions: trading volume declines in advance of new commission rules and then increases by 0.11–0.14% upon implementation. Both designs point to economically meaningful increases in trading activity, concentrated in more volatile stocks. We rationalize these findings with a mechanism in which fixed minimum commission schedules facilitate anti-competitive brokerage behavior: by limiting price competition, they increase the incentives and scope for brokers to steer naïve investors toward high-commission stocks, amplifying speculative trading precisely where volatility is highest.

- Question: How do brokerage commissions affect trading activity?
- Setting: NYSE minimum commission schedules before deregulation in 1975, set as a function of stock price
- Data: Historical NYSE commission schedules and stock trading volume
- Method: Regression kink design at schedule kinks; difference-in-differences around schedule revisions
- Trading volume response to a 1% rise in commissions: +0.15% to 0.40%
- Volume around schedule revisions: Falls before new rules, rises 0.11–0.14% on implementation
- Where effects concentrate: More volatile stocks
- Mechanism: Fixed schedules let brokers steer naïve investors toward high-commission stocks

Keywords: brokerage commissions, trading costs, trading volume, fixed commissions, NYSE, May Day 1975, market microstructure, broker incentives, volatility

BibTeX key: heimer2026brokerage

## Borrowing Young, Paying Later

Authors: Allison Cole, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Igor Livshits
Status: Working paper, draft available on request
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/borrowing-young-paying-later.html
Topics: Consumer credit and debt, Consumer protection and financial regulation, Mortgage lending and housing

In brief: Keeping young adults away from credit cards protected them from early defaults and raised their credit scores and homeownership by age 30, but led to more mortgage defaults. The paper studies the Credit CARD Act of 2009, which barred card issuance to people under 21 without a cosigner or verified income, and follows affected cohorts into their early thirties in credit bureau data. The Act cut early card ownership and severe delinquency, at the cost of a temporary credit score deficit in the early twenties. By age 30, affected individuals were 2 to 4 percentage points more likely to have prime or super-prime scores and 5 to 6 percentage points more likely to own a home. Their mortgages defaulted more often, however: people who never had a chance to reveal their credit risk on a card looked creditworthy on paper.

Abstract: Restricting credit access protects borrowers from financial mistakes, but limits the accumulation of credit history that lenders use to extend future credit. We study these competing forces using the Credit Card Accountability Responsibility and Disclosure (CARD) Act of 2009, which barred credit card issuance to individuals under age 21 without a cosigner or verified income. Exploiting cohort-based variation in exposure with an adjacent-cohorts design that controls for secular trends, we trace long-run credit outcomes using credit bureau data. The CARD Act reduced early card ownership and severe delinquency substantially, at the cost of a temporary credit score deficit in the early twenties. By age 30, treated individuals are 2–4 percentage points more likely to hold prime or super-prime credit scores and 5–6 percentage points more likely to own a home, but at the cost of increased mortgage delinquency. An instrumental variables decomposition reveals that protection from early delinquency drives the credit score and homeownership gains, while credit exclusion generates adverse selection into the mortgage market — borrowers who never had the opportunity to reveal their credit risk through card delinquency appear creditworthy on paper but default at elevated rates.

- Question: Does restricting young people’s access to credit help or hurt their long-run financial outcomes?
- Setting: The Credit CARD Act of 2009, which barred card issuance under age 21 without a cosigner or verified income
- Data: FRBNY Consumer Credit Panel / Equifax, followed through age 32
- Method: Adjacent-cohorts design benchmarked against placebo cohort pairs; instrumental variables decomposition
- Card ownership at age 18: −22 pp
- Severe card delinquency through the mid-twenties: −5 to −15 pp
- Prime or super-prime credit score at age 30: +2 to 4 pp
- Homeownership at age 30: +5 to 6 pp
- Severe delinquency among mortgage holders: +7.4 pp

Keywords: Credit CARD Act, young adults, credit card access, consumer credit, credit scores, homeownership, mortgage delinquency, adverse selection, credit bureau data

BibTeX key: heimer2026borrowing

## Waiting for Wealth: Inheritances and Household Savings

Authors: Eirik Eylands Brandsaas, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Mateo Velásquez-Giraldo
Status: Working paper, draft available on request
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/waiting-for-wealth-inheritances-household-savings.html
Topics: Saving, retirement, and inheritance

In brief: Inheritances, which account for a quarter to a half of U.S. household wealth, change how households save long before the money arrives. The paper adds inheritances to a standard life-cycle model of saving: households have a living parent whose wealth changes over time and who leaves an inheritance at death, with parental mortality, wealth, and the share lost to taxes and fees calibrated from the SCF, PSID, and HRS. Inheritances act as large, positive income shocks whose size, probability, and timing are all uncertain. Leaving them out makes the model overstate how patient households are. Including them raises consumption and its spread at all ages, mostly through anticipation, and raises wealth inequality among younger households. Households would pay substantial sums to receive their inheritance today, especially when their parents are wealthy.

Abstract: Inheritances account for a quarter to a half of U.S. household wealth, yet the canonical life-cycle model of saving omits them. We extend the model so that households have a living parent whose wealth evolves stochastically and who leaves an inheritance at death, and we calibrate parental mortality, parental wealth dynamics, and inheritance slippage using the SCF, PSID, and HRS. Inheritances generate large, positive income shocks whose probability, size, and timing are all uncertain. Omitting them leads to an overestimate of the discount factor (0.947 versus 0.933), a difference that compounds substantially over life-cycle horizons. Anticipated inheritances raise the level and dispersion of consumption at all ages, lower saving among younger households, and increase wealth inequality before about age 60. Consistent with the model, households with wealthier parents consume more, all else equal. Households would pay substantial amounts to receive their inheritance today, particularly when their parents are wealthy.

- Question: How do expected and realized inheritances shape household saving and consumption?
- Setting: A life-cycle model in which households have a living parent whose wealth evolves stochastically
- Data: SCF, PSID, and HRS, used to calibrate parental mortality, wealth, and inheritance slippage
- Method: Structural life-cycle model estimated with and without inheritances
- Estimated discount factor: 0.933 with inheritances versus 0.947 without
- Consumption of children of the wealthiest 20% of parents (PSID): About 10% higher, after controls
- Wealth inequality: Higher among households younger than about 60
- Willingness to pay to inherit today: Positive, and rising with parental wealth

Keywords: inheritances, bequests, life-cycle model, household saving, consumption, wealth inequality, discount factor, parental wealth, intergenerational transfers

BibTeX key: heimer2026waiting

## Are People Overconfident about Avoiding COVID-19?

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer, Haoyang Liu, and Xiaohan Zhang
Status: Liberty Street Economics, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (2020)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/overconfidence-avoiding-covid-19.html
Topics: Behavioral finance and beliefs

In brief: People expect their own exposure to COVID-19 to be much lower than the exposure they attribute to the general public. Using the New York Fed’s Survey of Consumer Expectations, the post documents a gap of 17.5 percentage points at a three-month horizon. The overconfidence is stronger among higher-income and younger households and fades over longer horizons.

Abstract: Using the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s Survey of Consumer Expectations, we document that people expect significantly lower personal exposure to COVID-19 than they attribute to the general public — a gap of 17.5 percentage points at the three-month horizon. This overconfidence is stronger among higher-income and younger households and fades over longer horizons. Overconfidence is distinct from absolute confidence: high-income respondents still perceive greater personal risk than low-income respondents, even while perceiving themselves as less exposed than the public. These behavioral biases may have contributed to the difficulty of containing the virus.

Keywords: overconfidence, COVID-19, risk perception, Survey of Consumer Expectations, subjective beliefs

## Intergenerational Homeownership and Mortgage Distress

Authors: Nicholas Fritsch and Rawley Z. Heimer
Status: Economic Commentary 2020-12, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2020)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/intergenerational-homeownership-mortgage-distress.html
Topics: Mortgage lending and housing

In brief: Children whose parents experienced mortgage distress during the 2008 financial crisis are less likely to buy a home. Motivated by research on how personal experiences shape financial attitudes, the commentary examines whether parents’ negative homeownership experiences in the financial crisis made their children view homeownership less favorably, and explores the channels behind the link.

Abstract: Rates of US homeownership have declined in the past two decades, and the decline has been especially pronounced for young adults. Motivated by recent research that explores the ways in which personal experiences can affect financial attitudes and beliefs, we explore whether the negative homeownership experiences of parents during the 2008 financial crisis could have caused their children to view homeownership less favorably. We find that parental mortgage distress negatively correlates with the probability that a child will purchase a home, and we explore various channels through which this link may occur.

Keywords: homeownership, mortgage distress, intergenerational transmission, young adults, 2008 financial crisis

## Geographic Mobility and Consumer Financial Health: Evidence from Oil Production Boom Towns

Authors: Rawley Z. Heimer, Timothy Stehulak, and Caitlin Treanor
Status: Economic Commentary 2016-13, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2016)
Page: https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/geographic-mobility-consumer-financial-health.html
Topics: Consumer credit and debt

In brief: Residents who leave oil boom towns after the bust have stronger consumer financial health than those who stay. Using the New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, the commentary follows residents of areas that saw a surge in oil drilling around 2010 and a bust afterward. Those who relocate after the bust have lower credit utilization, fewer delinquent accounts, and more new credit than those who stay.

Abstract: One way a household might handle financial distress is to relocate to another area that offers greater income opportunities. This article examines the impact of geographic mobility on consumer finances by focusing on the residents of “boom towns” — areas that saw a surge of growth in oil-drilling activity around 2010 and a bust thereafter. We find that residents who move after the bust experience stronger consumer financial health than residents who stay put.

Keywords: geographic mobility, consumer financial health, oil boom, credit utilization, delinquency, Consumer Credit Panel

BibTeX key: heimer2016mobility
